title: Practice: Introduction to Rates of Reaction

questions.stem: In a reaction between marble chips and hydrochloric acid, 60 cm³ of gas is collected in 30 seconds. What is the mean rate of reaction?
questions.explanation: Mean rate of reaction = amount of product formed / time taken = 60 cm³ / 30 s = 2 cm³/s. Rate of reaction measures how quickly products are formed (or reactants used up) over time. The units depend on what is measured - here it is volume of gas per second.

questions.stem: A graph of mass of product formed against time shows a curve that starts steep and gradually levels off. What does the levelling off indicate?

options.text: The reaction has finished - one of the reactants has been used up

questions.explanation: The curve levels off when the reaction is complete - the limiting reactant has been fully consumed. The steep initial part shows the fastest rate (when reactant concentrations are highest). As reactants are used up, the rate decreases until no more product can be formed and the line becomes horizontal.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT affect the rate of a chemical reaction?

options.text: The enthalpy change of the reaction

questions.explanation: The enthalpy change (Delta H) tells us how much energy is released or absorbed overall, but it does not determine how fast the reaction occurs. Rate is affected by temperature, concentration (or pressure for gases), surface area, and catalysts - all of which influence the frequency and energy of collisions between particles.

questions.stem: A student measures the rate of a reaction by recording the loss in mass over time using a balance. The reaction produces CO2 gas. After 5 minutes, the mass has decreased by 2.2 g. What is the mean rate of reaction?
questions.explanation: Mean rate = change in mass / time = 2.2 g / 5 min = 0.44 g/min. The mass decreases because CO2 gas escapes from the container. Note that option D (0.0073 g/s = 0.44/60) is the same rate in different units but was not the calculation asked for in g/min.

questions.stem: Food spoils more slowly in a refrigerator than at room temperature. How does this relate to rates of reaction?

options.text: Cold temperatures kill all bacteria, stopping reactions completely
Lower temperatures reduce the rate of chemical reactions that cause food to decompose
Refrigerators remove oxygen, preventing oxidation reactions
Refrigerators act as catalysts that slow down reactions

questions.explanation: Lower temperatures mean particles have less kinetic energy, so they collide less frequently and with less energy. Fewer collisions exceed the activation energy, so reactions (including bacterial metabolism and enzymatic breakdown of food) proceed more slowly. The reactions are not stopped, just slowed significantly.
